Incircle In Segment 1

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: Move the dots to change a curved slice with two circles inside it, and watch the line through the places where the circles cross.
How to play: Drag A, C or D, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Tick Hint for extra lines, then press New diagram or Reset.
Look for the math

Move the dots and the two circles change size and position. Yet whenever they cross, the line through the two crossing points keeps going through the same point M at the bottom of the big circle. Why?

How the circles are built

The big circle has centre O and a horizontal chord AB. The point M is the middle of the arc on the other side of the chord. For a touch point P on the chord, the applet projects O onto the line MP, reflects M in that projection to get Q, and puts the small circle's centre where the line OQ meets the vertical through P. That circle touches the chord at P and the big circle at Q, so M, P and Q lie on one line. This is the claim of the sibling applet IncircleInSegment, which uses a single circle and one touch point.

The number that stays the same

Write A = P and B = Q on that line through M. The page's identity is

MA × MB = MT2

Here T is either end of the chord; both ends are the same distance from M because the chord is horizontal. The left side is the power of M with respect to that inscribed circle, and the right side works out to 2 × (radius of C) × (distance from M up to the chord). It does not depend on where P sits on the chord. The logic test checks this on more than a thousand chord-and-contact configurations, to better than a billionth of the board's scale.

One line, two circles

Both inscribed circles give M the very same power, so M lies on their radical axis. For two circles that cross at U and V, that axis is exactly the line UV. Hence U, V and M are collinear — the page's claim (1), confirmed across the tested range. When the circles do not cross in two real points, the applet draws a fallback line from M toward the line joining the two centres; there is no U,V line to speak of then.

The hint, and a change from the Java applet

Tick Hint to see the circle centred at M through A. Where it meets a small circle, the line to M is a tangent, because the tangent length squared is the power MT2. The applet also draws lines from M to each contact and to B. The original page notes that the whole fact follows from inversion too. Two small deviations: this page stops A just short of the top and bottom of the circle, where the chord collapses; and it adds Reset and New diagram buttons the Java panel did not have. The live cut-the-knot page still embeds the Java applet, matching the archived class files, so no Wayback copy was needed.

Try dragging C until the two circles just touch: watch the green line stay straight through M. Then tick Hint and follow the tangents.
